112	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK_TITLE` | the task id / title (full body: `"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`) |
113	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_PROJECTS` | comma-separated projects this task spans |

117	## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)
118	
119	Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
120	The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:
121	
122	- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
123	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
124	  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
125	  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.
126	- If this is the run's **last round** (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` + 1 ==
127	  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS`), leave the workspace hand-off-clean: commit, update
128	  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
129	- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
130	  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).
131	
132	## One-shot discipline (important)
133	
134	This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
135	when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
136	(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
137	uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).
138	
139	## Pick the highest-value work
140	
141	Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
142	piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
143	infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
144	lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
145	you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.
146	
147	If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
148	task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
149	the objective is large. Leave a `"$HORIZON_BIN" task comment <task_id> --body …`
150	at each significant step. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
151	`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;
152	`blocked`/`failed` if genuinely stuck; set nothing if it's only partly advanced
153	(it returns to the queue).
154	
155	## Fresh-context checkpoints
156	
157	The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent
158	review is still part of convergence. Spawn the **`ground`** subagent at these
159	checkpoints:
160	
161	- before marking a multi-step task `done`;
162	- after every two substantive Horizon sessions on a long-running task;
163	- immediately after a strategy pivot, a broad workspace edit, or a surprising
164	  clean/build result.
165	
166	Give it the task/project scope and ask it to inspect the actual ledger diff,
167	blueprint graph, Lean state, roadmap, inbox, and reports with fresh context. It
168	is read-only on source and reports issues/memory; reconcile its findings before
169	continuing. Use **`work-reviewer`** for a narrow diff/proof audit and **`janitor`**
170	when the main concern is workspace hygiene. A one-session task may skip the
171	periodic checkpoint, but must still obtain a fresh-context review before a
172	terminal `done` claim.
173	
174	Schedule upkeep even when the last command did not print a warning. On a
175	multi-session run, dispatch **`janitor` at the start of every second Horizon
176	session** and before the final report; on a one-session task, dispatch it once
177	before claiming completion if the run touched roadmap, task, or inbox state.
178	Record the checkpoint in the report and wait for the helper before continuing.
179	If `janitor` is unavailable, ask **`ground`** for the same hygiene inspection;
180	Ground is read-only, so apply or explicitly record its findings yourself.
181	
182	## Warnings are work
183	
184	Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
185	warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
186	notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
187	the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
188	silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
189	address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that
190	survives your session should be one you *chose* to leave, with a trace saying
191	why.
192	
193	Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger, not background noise. When
194	`inbox`, `roadmap`, or `task` reports an overloaded queue, stale running item,
195	or status mismatch, pause the proof loop and spawn **`janitor`** with the
196	workspace scope. Wait for it, reconcile its report, rerun the command, and
197	record any warning that remains intentionally. Do this at most once for the
198	same warning in a session; a persistent warning still needs a report or inbox
199	issue rather than repeated no-op calls.

201	## Do the work (Lean)
202	
203	For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its
204	required LSP loop: query the target with `lean_diagnostic_messages` or
205	`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake
206	build` for the final session boundary or a specifically required kernel check;
207	LSP is enough between edits and proof obligations. Use the narrowest `lake env
208	lean` fallback when LSP is unavailable, and do not duplicate that check when the
209	configured final build covers the same files.
210	
211	**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
212	find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
213	afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in
214	mathlib — query it:
215	
216	| You want | Use | Not |
217	|---|---|---|
218	| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
219	| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |
220	| "what matches this *type*?" | LSP `lean_loogle` (`Nat → ?a → ?a`) | `grep` |
221	| "does something in scope close this goal?" | LSP `lean_local_search` / `lean_hover_info` | reading files |
222	| "what should I prove next?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` (ranked) | scanning the blueprint |
223	| "what does this node depend on / block?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:<id>` | reading imports |
224	| "is the proof right?" | `lake env lean <file>` (narrowest faithful check) | `lean_diagnostic_messages` alone |
225	
226	`"$HORIZON_BIN" search` covers **your projects and mathlib together**, which is
227	its whole point: the premise you need is usually already in mathlib under a name
228	you would never have grepped for. One query costs a second; re-proving an
229	existing lemma costs a session. If it reports a library as unindexed, fix that
230	first (`lake build`, then `"$HORIZON_BIN" search --reindex`) rather than falling
231	back to grep.
232	
233	Grep is still the right tool for what it *is* good at: finding a known string, a
234	specific file, or every call site of a name you already have.
235	
236	- Search before proving — the lemma may already exist. Skill: `leansearch`.
237	- Use the **Lean LSP MCP** for tight proof feedback, then verify with the narrowest
238	  faithful `lake` / `lake env lean` check. Skill: `lean-check`.
239	- Use the DAG to choose and scope work, not just to report it. Skill: `hgraph`.
240	- When editing blueprint material, follow the house format. Skill: `blueprint-conventions`.
241	  The blueprint is timeless mathematics, never a formalization journal. Put Lean
242	  implementation notes, failed tactics, and declaration-specific progress on the
243	  corresponding hgraph node with `graph add comment`; do not insert
244	  "Formalization note" paragraphs into blueprint `.tex` files.
245	
246	## Read the other projects
247	
248	They are in this workspace for a reason: the same lemma, pattern, or dead end has
249	often already been worked out next door. `"$HORIZON_BIN" search` spans **all**
250	projects — an existing construction in another project is a lead, whether you
251	import it, copy the approach, or read its blueprint. `references/` holds the
252	original sources (skill: `references`). Staying inside your own project because
253	the task named it is how the workspace re-derives the same thing three times.
254	
255	## Delegating beyond your team (ask permission first)
256	
257	Your normal way to parallelize is **within** your team: spawn subagents/workers
258	(skill: `subagents`) and dispatch scoped work to them in the foreground. That
259	needs no permission.
260	
261	Launching work **outside** your team — creating new tasks for other teams, or
262	spawning a whole new `horizon run` — is different: it spends the user's compute
263	and accounts, so it is **off by default**. Before you even consider it, read the
264	standing consent: `"$HORIZON_BIN" permissions --json`. It reports
265	`allow_launch_tasks`, `allow_launch_runs`, `max_parallel_sessions`, any declared
266	`accounts`, and free-form notes the user left (e.g. which account to prefer, when
267	limits reset). If both `allow_*` are false (the default), **do not** create tasks
268	or launch runs on the user's behalf — instead leave an inbox item `--to human`
269	proposing the delegation and why. Only when a flag is enabled may you act within
270	its stated caps, and follow the account/usage notes the user recorded.
271	
272	## Record progress = commit (this is how progress is read)
273	
274	Your commits — message + diff — are the durable record of what you did; the
275	dashboard reads progress from them. Commit coherent progress yourself with plain
276	`git` into the workspace ledger. Skill: `project-git` (use `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m …`
277	or the explicit `--git-dir/--work-tree` form; provenance trailers are auto-stamped).
278	
279	Write **semantic, math-first** messages that say what you proved/built. Prefer
280	staging explicit files over `add -A`. Beyond commits:
281	
282	- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status (`--status`) and strategy prose
283	  (`--summary`), not a re-narration of the diff.
284	- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
285	  as **memory**.
286	
287	Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
288	`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
289	strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
290	archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
291	remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
292	that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
293	shorter. In particular, review every open conversation your task started: archive
294	answered threads and leave a concrete blocker on any that must stay open. This
295	pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.
296	
297	## Resuming after an interruption
298	
299	State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
300	cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
301	the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:
302	
303	- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
304	  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
305	  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
306	  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
307	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
308	- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
309	  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
310	  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
311	  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
312	- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
313	  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
314	  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
315	  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
316	  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
317	  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
318	  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
319	  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.
320	
321	## Final report (your last message)
322	
323	Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
324	session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
325	Recommended sections: `## Summary`, `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
326	`## Why I stopped`, `## Next` (keep at least `## Progress` and
327	`## Why I stopped`). In `## Progress`, one inline `-` bullet per file/target,
328	e.g. `- FileA.lean: 4 sorries -> 3; closed the base case.` In `## Why I
329	stopped`, say plainly whether the objective is fully complete, partly advanced,
330	or blocked — and why. Always mention build failures, broken proofs, blocked
331	dependencies, and checks that failed or were not run. If a plausible next
332	action fits in the session's scope, take it before stopping — a clean commit is
333	not by itself a reason to stop.
334	
335	## Cleaning up the work (you decide, via subagents)
336	
337	There is no second orchestrator role running alongside you. *You* are the driver,
338	and the **`ground`** subagent is the scheduled fresh-context checkpoint when the
339	workspace or strategy needs an external view. Available helpers (see the

341	
342	- **janitor** — workspace hygiene: roadmap/READMEs concise, inbox from overflowing.
343	- **ground** — workspace-wide strategy, graph, ledger, and convergence review.
344	- **work-reviewer** — fresh-context review of your last work; is it converging?
345	- **blueprint** — Lean ↔ blueprint statement/`\uses` correctness for a scoped slice.
346	- **reference-retriever**, **debug**, **page-transcriber** — as needed.
347

1	# Concurrent-lane protocol (2026-07-16, from inbox I-0149's incidents — BINDING for parallel agent fleets)
2	
3	Adopted after the 2026-07-16 evening wave's four incidents (I-0149). These rules extend the
4	standing handoff protocol (07-14/14b/15) for any session running two or more lanes in this
5	workspace.
6	
7	## 1. Ledger commits: private index + compare-and-swap (the shared-index race)
8	
9	All lanes commit through one `workspace.git`; concurrent `git add`+`commit` through the
10	SHARED index can interleave and record spurious deletions of another lane's
11	freshly-committed files (happened in `6197c9676`, 862 lines vanished from HEAD, restored
12	byte-identical in `a640fef5b`). Concurrent lanes MUST commit via a private index:
13	
14	```bash
15	cd /home/axel/LeanAlgebraicGeometry-Horizon
16	GD=.archon-horizon/vcs/workspace.git
17	export GIT_INDEX_FILE=$(mktemp)
18	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. read-tree HEAD
19	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. add <ONLY your paths…>
20	TREE=$(git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. write-tree)
21	PARENT=$(git --git-dir=$GD rev-parse HEAD)
22	COMMIT=$(git --git-dir=$GD -c user.name="Archon Horizon" -c user.email="archon-horizon@local" \
23	  commit-tree $TREE -p $PARENT -m "<math-first message>
24	
25	Archon-Commit: agent
26	Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>")
27	git --git-dir=$GD update-ref refs/heads/main $COMMIT $PARENT   # CAS: fails if HEAD moved
28	unset GIT_INDEX_FILE
29	```
30	
31	If the `update-ref` CAS fails (HEAD moved), re-read HEAD and repeat — never force.
32	ALWAYS verify afterward: `git --git-dir=$GD show --stat HEAD` must touch only your paths.
33	A single-lane session may keep the plain `add`+`commit` recipe, but must still verify.
34	
35	### 1a. THE RECIPE ABOVE HAS A RACE — read HEAD ONCE, not twice (2026-07-28, run 0072)
36	
37	**As written, the recipe reads `HEAD` twice**: once in `read-tree HEAD`, and again several lines
38	later in `PARENT=$(… rev-parse HEAD)`. If another lane's CAS lands **between those two reads**,
39	your tree is built from the *old* snapshot while your parent is the *new* commit — and
40	`update-ref` **succeeds**, because it only checks that the ref has not moved since `rev-parse`.
41	It never checks that the tree was built from that ref. You publish a stale tree, silently
42	reverting everything that landed in the window.
43	
44	**Measured once, and the measurement is narrow — do not over-read it.** `e964967e8` has parent
45	`a1ef4d59c` and, diffed against *that parent*, deletes 95 lines of
46	`informal/w4-rep-critical-path.md`, 52 of `informal/w5-t4-worksheet.md` and 19 of
47	`Picard/Pic0ChartLocusIsOpen.lean` — exactly the restore `a1ef4d59c` had just performed, undone.
48	Its `read-tree` ran before `a1ef4d59c` landed; its parent was captured after. It staged explicit
49	paths and the pathspec *was* honoured: **the sweep came from the TREE BASE, not the pathspec**,
50	which is why "stage explicit files" is not a defence and why the symptom is indistinguishable
51	from §1b's shared-index staleness.
52	
53	**Two other lanes audited their own CAS commits the same day (fifteen commits between them,
54	recipe verbatim) and found zero reverts.** That is consistent with this: the race only fires when
55	another lane's CAS lands inside your particular window, so clean commits are the expected
56	outcome, not evidence of absence. The discriminating question is not "did my commits look clean"
57	but "was my `read-tree` separated from my `rev-parse` by somebody else's commit". Treat §1a as
58	cheap insurance, not as a diagnosis of every mystery revert — and check §1b too.
59	
60	**The fix is one line — capture the parent BEFORE the tree, and read-tree that sha:**
61	
62	```bash
63	PARENT=$(git --git-dir=$GD rev-parse HEAD)     # ONCE, up front
64	export GIT_INDEX_FILE=$(mktemp)
65	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. read-tree $PARENT      # not "HEAD"
66	git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. add <ONLY your paths…>
67	TREE=$(git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. write-tree)
68	COMMIT=$(git --git-dir=$GD … commit-tree $TREE -p $PARENT -m "…")
69	git --git-dir=$GD update-ref refs/heads/main $COMMIT $PARENT   # now genuinely atomic
70	```
71	
72	Then a mid-recipe CAS by another lane makes `update-ref` **fail**, you re-read and retry, and the
73	protocol behaves as it was meant to. The verification step ("must touch only your paths") is what
74	catches it after the fact — run it every time, and read the file list, not just the count.
75	
76	### 1b. The CAS recipe leaves the SHARED index permanently stale — this is by design, and it is armed
77	
78	Added 2026-07-27 (run 0048 r5) after this failed a **third** time (`I-0366`: the shared index
79	was pinned to a pre-round-5 snapshot and a bare `git commit` would have deleted
80	`Picard/JacobianDataCharts.lean` and un-rooted it from `AlgebraicJacobian.lean` in one commit).
81	
82	The mechanism is not a bug in anyone's lane, it is the direct consequence of §1: a CAS commit
83	publishes a tree built in a **private** `GIT_INDEX_FILE` and moves the ref with `update-ref`.
84	The **shared** index is never touched, so the moment anybody commits, the shared index still
85	describes the previous HEAD — and `git status` then reports that difference as *staged changes*,
86	including **staged deletions** for any file the commit added. The longer a run goes, the further
87	the shared index drifts behind.
88	
89	Consequences, all three binding:
90	
91	1. **Never run a bare `git commit` (no `-a`, no pathspec) against `workspace.git`.** It publishes
92	   whatever the stale shared index holds, which is a reversion of other lanes' work.
93	2. **Before finishing, check and repair.** `git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. status --porcelain | grep '^D'`
94	   must be empty. If it is not, repair with the **narrowest** form that covers your paths:
95	   `git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. reset -q -- <your project dir>/`. Prefer this to a whole-index
96	   `read-tree HEAD` when another run is live — a full reset can discard the other run's staging.
97	3. **Verify the worktree is the good copy before repairing.** `reset` makes the index match HEAD;
98	   that is only safe once you have confirmed the on-disk file is the one you want
99	   (`diff <(git --git-dir=$GD cat-file -p HEAD:<path>) <path>`).
100	
101	Expect to repeat step 2 more than once in a long session: every CAS commit by any lane re-stales
102	the index, so a repair done early does not stay done.
103	
104	## 2. The lake mutex is a mkdir DIRECTORY lock — never flock a file there
105	
106	`/tmp/claude-1001/ajcr-locks/lake.lock` is acquired by `mkdir` (atomic; a crash leaves a
107	directory that the next holder's timeout logic can reap). It is NOT a flock file: a lane
108	that runs `flock /tmp/claude-1001/ajcr-locks/lake.lock …` creates a plain FILE at the
109	path, and every mkdir-acquire loop then spins forever (this deadlocked all lanes
110	15:18–19:10 on 2026-07-16 until a human deleted it). Acquire pattern:
111	
112	```bash
113	LOCK=/tmp/claude-1001/ajcr-locks/lake.lock
114	while ! mkdir "$LOCK" 2>/dev/null; do
115	  # (a) plain FILE at the path = a flock protocol-violation; reap immediately.
116	  if [ -f "$LOCK" ]; then echo "STALE: plain file at $LOCK (flock violation) — removing" >&2; rm -f "$LOCK"; continue; fi
117	  # (b) orphaned DIRECTORY from a crashed build (rmdir never ran). Reap on proof of death:
118	  if [ -d "$LOCK" ]; then
119	    holder=$(cat "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null)
120	    if [ -n "$holder" ] && ! kill -0 "$holder" 2>/dev/null; then
121	      echo "STALE: holder pid $holder dead — reaping" >&2; rm -rf "$LOCK"; continue
122	    fi
123	    # No pidfile (old-cohort holder): reap only if NO live lake build AND the dir is >15 min old.
124	    if [ -z "$holder" ] && ! pgrep -f 'lake build AlgebraicJacobian' >/dev/null 2>&1 \
125	       && [ $(( $(date +%s) - $(stat -c %Y "$LOCK" 2>/dev/null || date +%s) )) -gt 900 ]; then
126	      echo "STALE: no live build, lock >15min old — reaping" >&2; rm -rf "$LOCK"; continue
127	    fi
128	  fi
129	  sleep 10
130	done
131	echo $$ > "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null      # record holder so a later reaper can prove liveness via kill -0
132	# … lake build … ; rm -rf "$LOCK"      # release (rm -rf, not rmdir — the pidfile makes the dir non-empty)
133	```
134	
135	### 2a. THE RELEASE IS AS DANGEROUS AS THE REAP — check the pidfile before `rm -rf` (2026-07-28, run 0072)
136	
137	The acquire loop above is careful; the release (`rm -rf "$LOCK"`) is not, and that asymmetry
138	caused a real incident. **A lane removed the lock directory while its pidfile named a LIVE pid
139	belonging to another lane's build**, having printed `ALIVE` for that pid one line earlier.
140	
141	The mechanism is worth stating because nothing in the recipe warns about it. The offending lane
142	had legitimately acquired the lock, and then **its own shell was killed by a harness timeout
143	while it held it**. On the next turn it reasoned "the lock is mine and my holder is dead, so
144	release it" — but in the interval a *different* lane had acquired the lock, so the pid in the
145	file had never been its own. The lane was running the release branch on a belief about history
146	rather than on a reading of the file.
147	
148	> **Before `rm -rf "$LOCK"`, verify the pidfile still names YOUR pid.**
149	> `[ "$(cat "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null)" = "$$" ] && rm -rf "$LOCK"`
150	> If it names anything else, the lock is not yours to release: say so and leave it alone.
151	
152	Two corollaries:
153	
154	* **"It was mine a minute ago" is not evidence**, especially when a harness can kill the shell
155	  between acquire and release. Every turn boundary is a window for another lane to take the lock.
156	* **Do not "repair" the mistake by re-creating the directory with the other lane's pid.**
157	  Fabricating a pidfile for a build you do not own makes the lock unreapable by its real owner
158	  and hides the incident. Report it on the thread and let the owner re-take it.
159	
160	For long builds, prefer a form that cannot outlive its own hold: run the build detached with a
161	release trailing it in the *same* script, so the release is not a separate turn.
162	
163	Two stale shapes, both now handled above (do NOT just `sleep` forever on either):
164	- A plain FILE at the lock path is by definition stale (mkdir makes directories) — reap immediately.
165	- An orphaned DIRECTORY from a build that crashed before `rm -rf` (the 2026-07-19 C4 incident,
166	  I-0257): the OLD acquire loop only checked for a file, so it spun forever on this. Writing
167	  `$$` into `$LOCK/pid` on acquire lets the next lane prove the holder is dead (`kill -0`) and reap
168	  safely; the no-pidfile branch (a holder from before this fix) falls back to "no live build + >15min".
169	  Never reap a directory whose pidfile names a LIVE pid — that is a real build in progress.
170	
171	## 3. /tmp quota with >3 lanes
172	
173	uid-1001 tmpfs quota exhaustion (EDQUOT) bricked every Bash call machine-wide
174	(~19:00–19:20). With more than ~3 concurrent lanes, keep scratch artifacts small, clean up
175	build temp dirs, and if Bash starts failing with quota errors, stop and report rather than
176	retry-looping.
177	
178	## 4. The root import file: commit only your own lines (I-0153)
179	
180	`AlgebraicJacobian.lean` is edited by every lane. Committing the WHOLE file via any recipe
181	sweeps siblings' uncommitted import lines into HEAD — the root then references files not yet
182	in HEAD (red for fresh checkouts), and a later sibling's whole-file commit can sweep or drop
183	YOUR line the same way. Before committing the root file: run
184	`git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. diff HEAD -- <project>/AlgebraicJacobian.lean` — if lines
185	other than yours differ, either (a) verify every swept import's file is already committed in
186	HEAD and say so in the commit message, or (b) construct the commit from HEAD's version plus
187	only your lines (apply a minimal patch to a temp checkout of the HEAD blob). Never commit a
188	root file that references uncommitted files without naming that in the message.
189	
190	### 4a. A MINUS line in that diff is never yours (2026-07-28, run 0072)
191	
192	The check above works. The failure mode is **misreading** it, and it happened again on
193	2026-07-28: the diff printed a `-import`/`+import` pair from a sibling lane's *uncommitted*
194	worktree edit, the committing lane read it as background noise, and the commit published the
195	sibling's replacement — dropping `Picard/DivRepAffPullIndep.lean` from the import closure.
196	The file stayed in HEAD and still compiled, but was reachable from nothing: **un-rooted**,
197	i.e. I-0153 again, from a lane that had run the I-0153 check.
198	
199	So state the rule in a form that needs no judgement:
200	
201	> **A `-import` line in that diff is never yours.** The only clean result is `+import <your
202	> file>` and nothing else. Any minus line means you are about to delete another lane's root
203	> entry — stop and explain it before committing. An unexplained `+import` you did not write
204	> is the same signal: a sibling's uncommitted edit is in your worktree copy, and a minus line
205	> usually accompanies it.
206	
207	This is strictly stronger than "commit only your own lines", because you can intend that and
208	still sweep — staging the whole file is what publishes their edit, and the diff is your only
209	warning.
210	
211	**Repair additively, never by reverting.** Restore the dropped import while **keeping** the
212	other lane's new one, then verify with a full root build (the 2026-07-28 repair: 9139 jobs,
213	exit 0, with the un-rooted file rebuilt). Reverting to your own earlier root blob discards
214	their work and turns one incident into two.
215	
216	## 5. The AJCR mutex is for AJCR lake invocations only
217	
218	No cross-workspace use (an OpenGA-Horizon agent squatted it ~25 min for its own
219	`lake cache get`, silently serializing AJCR lanes against unrelated work). Other
220	workspaces must use their own lock paths.
221	
222	### 5a. Read it as per-PROJECT, not per-workspace (2026-07-28, run 0072)
223	
224	The rule above says "cross-workspace", and that wording has a hole: **AJC and AJCR are two
225	projects in the SAME workspace.** Observed live on 2026-07-28 — the AJCR mutex was held for
226	over ten minutes while the only live `lake build` belonged to an `ajc-*` lane building
227	`MainProjects/Algebraic-Jacobian-Challenge`, the sibling project. Same failure as the
228	OpenGA incident, not covered by the rule as written.
229	
230	The lock path is `ajcr-locks`, so read the rule as: **only lanes building
231	`Algebraic-Jacobian-Challenge-Rebuild` may take it.** AJC lanes need their own path
232	(`/tmp/claude-1001/ajc-locks/lake.lock`). Note the AJC task prompts do not mention a mutex
233	at all, which is very likely why an AJC lane reached for this one.
234	
235	### 5b. Write the pidfile — the no-pidfile fallback cannot distinguish squatter from orphan
236	
237	§2's acquire recipe writes `$$` into `$LOCK/pid` so a later lane can prove death via
238	`kill -0`. In the incident above the lock directory had **no pidfile**, so that branch could
239	not fire and the fallback ("no live `lake build AlgebraicJacobian` **and** dir >15 min old")
240	also could not fire — there *was* a live build, just not an AJCR one. Net effect: a
241	provably-non-AJCR holder is unreapable for 15 minutes.
242	
243	Two consequences for a blocked lane, both applied in that incident:
244	
245	* **Do not reap a directory whose holder you cannot prove dead**, even when you suspect a
246	  squatter. Reaping mid-build is worse than waiting.
247	* **Fall back to the narrowest check instead of blocking.** `lake env lean <file>` on the
248	  single changed file writes no shared build state and needs no lock; it is a faithful
249	  kernel check for that file. Record in the report that the mutex was unavailable and which
250	  check you substituted.
